title: Rebuilding the Ka'bah
era: The Stone No One Could Lift Alone
teaser: Four or five days, daggers half-drawn over who would lift one stone. Then a man of thirty-five walked in.

layers.title: Nine Cubits and a Flood
layers.subtitle: A small roofless House with cracked walls
layers.content:
The House they were about to take apart was small. Al-Mubarakpuri describes it as a low building of white stones, standing no more than nine arm's lengths, still on the plan it had held since the days of Isma'il. It had no roof, and that was the practical problem: the treasures kept inside could be reached by anyone willing to climb, and thieves had done exactly that. The walls had also been standing in open weather for a very long time. They were cracked and weakened by it.

Then came the water. Five years before the advent of prophethood a great flood ran through Makkah and swept towards the Ka'bah, and it came close to bringing the building down. After that the Quraysh had no choice. The sanctity of the place was the basis of their standing among the Arabs, and the structure carrying that sanctity was failing.

Before a single stone was moved, the chiefs made a decision about money that deserves to be stated plainly. They ruled that only lawful wealth would go into the rebuilding. Anything derived from immoral means, from usury, or from unjust dealing was kept out of the fund. These were men who prayed to idols. No scripture had told them to do this. They did it because they understood that this particular building could not be paid for with just any money.

Then the work had to begin, and nobody wanted to swing first. Knocking a hole in the wall of the Sacred House was not something men did casually. Al-Walid bin al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi took the first blow. When the others saw that nothing happened to him, they joined in, and the demolition went on until they struck the foundation Ibrahim had laid.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — Rebuilding Al-Ka'bah and the Arbitration Issue

layers.title: Stone by Stone, Tribe by Tribe
layers.subtitle: A Roman mason and a man carrying rocks
layers.content:
With the old walls down, the work was parcelled out by tribe. Each clan took responsibility for a section of the wall, collected its own stones, and built. The man who actually laid them was a hired professional: a Roman mason named Baqum. The sirah keeps his name, which is a detail worth noticing. The most sacred building in Arabia went up by tribal labour under a foreign craftsman.

He was thirty-five, and he was one of the men hauling stone. Sahih al-Bukhari, in its chapter on the building of the Ka'bah, carries the account from Jabir bin Abdullah. He was working alongside his uncle al-Abbas, and al-Abbas told him to fold his loincloth up over his shoulder to keep the stones off his skin. He did it. He fell to the ground, and his eyes turned skyward. Then he came round and called out for his loincloth, and covered himself again. A further report adds that his loins were never seen after that day.

There was no message yet, no prophethood, no law. What is recorded here is an instinctive refusal, reported through a chain of narration rather than reconstructed by historians — one of the very few times we see him at work in these years through the eyes of hadith.

Al-Mubarakpuri adds one more fact about the construction, and it makes the next layer land harder: the work went on in harmony. Rival clans, competing interests, a single shared wall, and no trouble whatsoever. Right up to the last piece.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, chapter on the building of the Ka'bah, narrated by Jabir bin Abdullah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Sahih Al-Bukhari 1/540

layers.title: The Last Piece
layers.subtitle: Five days of deadlock over one black stone
layers.content:
The last piece was the Black Stone.

It had to go back into the corner of the new wall, and every chief in Makkah wanted to be the man who put it there. The honour could not be divided and there were far too many claimants. The dispute ran, al-Mubarakpuri writes, for four or five days. Positions hardened. Daggers were on the point of being drawn and serious bloodshed looked imminent. Men who had just finished building a wall together were now close to killing each other over a single stone, in the courtyard of the House they had rebuilt in order to protect its sanctity.

What broke the deadlock was a procedural suggestion from the oldest man present. Abu Umaiyah bin al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi proposed that they let the first person to enter the Sanctuary decide the question. Everyone accepted it, for the good reason that nobody could arrange the outcome in advance.

The first man through the gate was Muhammad ﷺ. The crowd's response is preserved as one shout with one voice: al-Amin has come, and we are content to abide by his decision. The name his city had already settled on him did the work before he had said anything at all.

They put the deadlock to him. He asked for a mantle. He spread it on the ground and set the Black Stone in the middle of it. Then he called forward a representative of each clan, had every one of them take hold of the cloth, and told them to lift together. They carried the stone to the corner as a single body. When it reached the place it was to occupy, he took it in his own hands and set it in position.

Nobody lost. That was the entire design of the solution.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 2/192-197 and Tarikh At-Tabari 2/289

layers.title: What Was Left Out
layers.subtitle: No ayah, and a hadith about the shortfall
layers.content:
No revelation came down about the rebuilding. He was thirty-five, five years short of the cave, and there was no Qur'an yet to comment on anything.

What the Qur'an would later do is name the thing the demolition crews had been digging towards. When they reached the bottom they stopped at a foundation the sirah identifies as Ibrahim's: «وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ» — 'And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il' (2:127). And it fixed the standing of the site itself: «إِنَّ أَوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ لَلَّذِي بِبَكَّةَ مُبَارَكًا» — 'Indeed, the first House established for mankind was the one at Bakkah, blessed' (3:96).

The sharpest commentary on this chapter, though, is a hadith, and it arrives decades afterwards.

The Quraysh ran out of lawful money before the walls were done. Rather than finish the House with wealth they had excluded on principle, they shortened the building. They left out an area of about six arm's lengths on the northern side — the space known as al-Hijr, or al-Hateem — and they lifted the door up off the ground so that entry could be controlled and only those they favoured admitted.

Aishah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said he would have pulled the Ka'bah down and rebuilt it on the foundation of Ibrahim, taking back into it what had been left out and setting its door level with the ground, and that the only thing stopping him was that her people would not accept it. That is in Sahih Muslim, in the Book of Hajj.

He knew precisely what that shortage of clean money had cost. He also judged that correcting it was not worth what the correction would cost the people.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 2:127 — «وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ» 'And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il'; see also 3:96
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, narrated by Aishah — the Prophet ﷺ on rebuilding the Ka'bah on Ibrahim's foundation
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj

layers.title: The Shape the Shortage Left
layers.subtitle: Measurements, a raised door, and a spread cloak
layers.content:
The building that stood when they finished was roughly square and about fifteen metres high. The side holding the Black Stone and the side opposite ran about ten metres each; the other two about twelve. The stone sat around a metre and a half above the level of the circumambulation. The door was two metres off the ground. Around the base ran a low ledge, a quarter of a metre high and about a third of a metre wide, called ash-Shadherwan, which al-Mubarakpuri notes was originally part of the Sanctuary and which the Quraysh also left outside their new wall.

Every one of those figures records a decision. The height is ambition. The raised door is exclusion, since it let the custodians admit only whom they chose. Al-Hijr and the Shadherwan are the marks left by a fund that ran dry because it refused to take dirty money.

The Black Stone he set with his hands that day is the one pilgrims still face. And the ruling on how to think about it came from Umar ibn al-Khattab, in Sahih al-Bukhari's Book of Hajj: he kissed it and said out loud, in front of the crowd, that he knew it was only a stone which could neither benefit nor harm, and that he was kissing it for one reason only — because he had seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kiss it.

What to carry out of this chapter is the mantle. He was handed a dispute in which every party had a genuine claim and none could be satisfied without humiliating the rest. He did not pick a winner and he did not split the difference. He redesigned the task so that the honour could be shared without being reduced: every clan's hand on the same cloth, the stone arriving by common effort, and the final placement done by the one man none of them would resent.

He was thirty-five. He held no office. He had nothing but a reputation, and he was already the only man in Makkah all of them would obey.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj, narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab — 'I know that you are only a stone'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj

quiz.prompt: Why did the Quraysh decide the Ka'bah had to be rebuilt?

options.text: A fire had destroyed its roof and the interior
It was low and roofless with cracked walls, and a great flood five years before prophethood nearly brought it down
An earthquake had split its eastern wall
A rival sanctuary had been built in Ta'if and they wanted a grander one

quiz.scholar_reflection: No roof meant thieves could reach the treasures inside. Age had weakened the walls. The flood turned a long-standing problem into an urgent one.

quiz.prompt: What rule did the chiefs of Quraysh set about the money that would fund the rebuilding?

options.text: Every clan would contribute an equal share regardless of wealth
The whole cost would be met from pilgrim revenues
Only lawful wealth would be used — money from immoral means, usury or unjust dealing was excluded
The wealthiest clan would fund it in exchange for custody of the keys

quiz.scholar_reflection: They were idolaters and had no revealed law obliging them to it. They held to the rule far enough that the money ran out and the House came out smaller than planned.

quiz.prompt: Who proposed the method that ended the standoff over the Black Stone, and what was it?

options.text: Al-Walid bin al-Mughirah — that lots should be drawn between the clans
Abu Umaiyah bin al-Mughirah, the oldest of the chiefs — that the first person to enter the Sanctuary should decide
Abu Talib — that the honour belonged to the clan with the oldest custody
Baqum the mason — that the stone be left out of the wall entirely

quiz.scholar_reflection: The proposal worked because it could not be fixed in advance. Nobody knew who would walk in next, so everybody could accept the result.

quiz.prompt: How did he settle the dispute once the chiefs had put it to him?

options.text: He assigned the honour to Banu Hashim, his own clan
He ordered the chiefs to draw lots and abide by the outcome
He placed the stone on a spread mantle, had a representative of every clan lift it together, and then set it in position with his own hands
He carried the stone alone and placed it without consulting anyone

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: Every clan's hand was on the cloth for the whole distance. The honour was made shareable rather than awarded.

quiz.prompt: Why did the Quraysh leave out the northern area known as al-Hijr, or al-Hateem?

options.text: Because Ibrahim's foundation did not extend into it
Because the flood had left that ground unsafe to build on
Because Baqum the mason advised against including it
Because they ran out of the lawful money they had collected

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar; and Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, narrated by Aishah
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ later said he would have rebuilt the House on Ibrahim's foundation and taken that area back in, and that only his people's unreadiness stopped him.

quiz.prompt: Idolaters ruled that no unlawful wealth would go into the House, then honoured that rule even when it meant building something smaller than they intended. What do you make of that?

options.text: They had a real sense of the sacred, even while worshipping stones
A principle that costs you something is the only kind that has been tested
It complicates the picture — the men who later opposed the message were not simply villains
All of these, and the shortened wall is the receipt

quiz.slider_label: How far will you let a principle cost you before you drop it?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the decision to exclude unlawful wealth
quiz.scholar_reflection: The gap in the wall is still there. It is the most honest piece of accounting in the whole structure.

quiz.prompt: For four or five days grown men nearly killed one another over who would lift a single stone. What was that dispute actually about?

options.text: Honour, which in that society was a harder currency than money
Precedence — a clan raised above the others inside the Sanctuary is above them everywhere else
Nothing of substance, which is exactly why it was so dangerous
All of these, and the men involved had just finished building a wall together

quiz.slider_label: How often is your last argument really about the thing you argued over?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the strife among the chiefs
quiz.scholar_reflection: They had cooperated flawlessly through the demolition and the whole rebuild. The fight came at the last piece, when there was finally something indivisible to claim.

quiz.prompt: His solution gave nobody the honour alone and everybody a hand on the cloth. Where in your own life would that move help?

options.text: Most deadlocks are about who is seen to win, not about the outcome itself
Redesigning the task beats adjudicating between the claims
It only worked because the arbitrator was trusted first — the reputation had to exist before the ruling
All of these, though the last one is the hardest to arrange

quiz.slider_label: Do you look for the winning argument or the shared one?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the mantle and the representatives of the clans
quiz.scholar_reflection: He could have taken the honour himself. He was the one man in the city no one would have contested. He gave it to all of them and kept only the placing.

quiz.prompt: He was accepted as arbitrator on the strength of a name his city had given him, with no office and no authority behind it. What builds standing like that?

options.text: Years of small dealings in which he had nothing to gain by being honest
It cannot be constructed deliberately — it is a conclusion other people reach about you
It was also fragile: within a decade that same city would be trying to be rid of him
All of these, which is why the shout at the gate is worth pausing on

quiz.slider_label: Whose verdict on you would you accept as accurate?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'Al-Amin has come; we are content to abide by his decision'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nobody proposed him. They had agreed to accept whoever walked in, and when it was him the objections stopped before they started.

quiz.prompt: He said he would have restored the House to Ibrahim's foundation, and then did not, because the people were not ready for it. What does that restraint teach?

options.text: Being right about a change is not the same as it being the moment for it
He weighed the disruption against the correction and let the correction go
Some inherited wrongs are left standing deliberately, and that is a decision rather than a failure
All of these — and he named the reason out loud instead of pretending the shortfall did not exist

quiz.slider_label: When have you been right and still chosen to wait?
quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, narrated by Aishah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had the authority to do it and the reason to do it. He said plainly what he would have done, and then left the wall where the Quraysh had put it.
